items.text:
Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
- Published
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.
The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:
- assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child
- engaging in organised criminal activity
- radicalisation
- facilitating the commission of a terrorist act
- being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.
- Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders 
  - Published19 October
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.
"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.
When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.
Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.
"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."
The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Additional reporting by Thomas Mukhwana

items.title: Spain’s Pedro Sanchez bets on left-wing voting surge to defy election polls
items.summary:
Spain’s Pedro Sanchez bets on left-wing voting surge to defy election polls
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez makes last bid to beat right-wing parties before Spanish vote on Sunday.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears sure he will secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election on Sunday
items.text:
Spain’s Pedro Sanchez bets on left-wing voting surge to defy election polls
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez makes last bid to beat right-wing parties before Spanish vote on Sunday.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears sure he will secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election on Sunday, despite adverse public polling suggesting a right-wing advantage.
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” the Socialist leader told radio station SER on Friday, as political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning before the vote.
The outcome of the election will be closely watched as Europe opens an electoral cycle over the next 12 months that could reshape the balance of power within the European Union.
Amid a legal ban on publishing opinion surveys within five days of an election, Sanchez insisted that internal data suggested his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.
He said that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching ‌a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.
However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party (PP) and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.
Choice between ‘regression and progressivism’
Earlier, during a televised pre-election debate, Sanchez clashed with PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo and Vox’s Santiago Abascal, as well as Ada Colau, a left-wing Spanish politician and former mayor of Barcelona associated with the Sumar political alliance, in a debate focused on immigration, the housing crisis and foreign policy.
The prime minister criticised the Madrid regional government, controlled by the PP, for awarding an honorary medal to the Israeli government while the assault on Gaza continued.
“It is shameful,” Sanchez said, accusing his opponents of having “no humanity whatsoever.”
He also interrupted Feijoo when the conservative leader described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “massacre”, insisting that “it is genocide”.
Sanchez warned voters that Spain faced a choice between “regression and progressivism”, arguing that the PP and Vox wanted to replicate the politics of US President Donald Trump and Argentinian President Javier Milei.
Sanchez has vaunted his record on the international stage, notably his outspoken defence of immigration, clashes with Trump and criticism of Israel. The dynamism of the EU’s fourth-largest economy under his leadership has also drawn praise at a turbulent time for global markets.
But a polarising status at home puts his tenure in peril.
‘Day of reflection’
Sanchez is holding his final large rally in Madrid on Friday, seeking a late mobilisation of left-wing voters to defeat what he calls the “regression” of a possible PP-Vox coalition.
“We are unstoppable and we will win!” he told a Socialist meeting in the western city of Plasencia, sporting a red T-shirt emblazoned with the slogan “the power of women”.
He contrasted a Spain “of prosperity, principles and values” against a “reactionary coalition” that would question women’s rights, cut pensions and gut public services.
PP leader Feijoo, who won the most seats at the last election in 2023 but failed to form a government, told supporters in Barcelona: “This time we will pull it off.”
Dismissing Sanchez’s campaign of “fear”, he will hold his campaign finale in Seville, capital of the southern Andalusia region.
Addressing reporters before a closing rally in the eastern city of Valencia, Vox leader Abascal accused Sanchez’s “mafia-style” government of “betraying, robbing and lying” to the country.
Spaniards will observe a “day of reflection” on the ‌eve ‌of the vote on Saturday. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.

items.text:
‘Bear trap’: Ukraine hails new operation as Russian casualties mount
Russian assaults met with stout defence along the front as Western powers discuss ceasefire proposals.
Ukraine’s forces liberated more of their land as Russia broke new casualty records and United States negotiators tried to convince Kyiv to give up territory, or NATO membership.
Details emerged on November 20 of a new operation – the fourth this year – in which Ukraine said it cleared Russian troops out of hundreds of square kilometres of land they occupied, this time in the northern Kharkiv region.
That was about a month after Russia said it had encircled 2,000 Ukrainian troops in an enclave adjacent to the Russian border, around the town of Velykyi Burluk.
Ukrainian commanders realised that the troops were in danger of being encircled, and ordered the execution of “Operation Bear Trap”, which relied on deceptive moves and secrecy to attack the enemy from various sides, concealing its main direction.
Ukrainian forces used a Russian T-80 tank and an Abrams M-1 tank to attack the border town of Vilhuvatka, giving the impression that their main blow would land there.
They then attacked Russian reinforcements from the rear as they arrived to shore up defences, and used drones to remotely mine Russian resupply routes.
The Ukrainian command said Operation Bear Trap has so far succeeded in liberating 200sq km (77sq miles) and 14 settlements, and was ongoing.
Russian troops continue to occupy at least four border villages in Kharkiv, including Vovchansk, but their plan to seize almost 500sq km (193sq miles) has been foiled.
It is not the first time Ukrainian forces preempted a Russian pincer movement.
Earlier this year they stopped an attempted encirclement of the “fortress belt” of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk and Druzhivka in the eastern Donetsk region during Operation Vivaldi.
But Kyiv still struggled to defend its skies and nationwide power outages are making life miserable for Ukrainians.
Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces in Donetsk were engaged in active defence, stopping attempted assaults and destroying vehicles.
Retired Ukrainian colonel Konstantyn Mashovets, who analyses the front on his Telegram channel, said Kyiv’s forces had also advanced in southern Zaporizhia, clearing Russian infiltrators out of the northern bank of the Solona river near Novopavlivka.
As Russia continued these assaults, its casualties rose to a record on November 24 of 432,519, Ukraine’s military said. The next day, it set a new monthly record of 55,629 for November, with five days to go in the month.
Despite Ukraine’s battlefield achievements, US mediation offers remained unchanged.
US negotiators had put two proposals before Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, citing people involved in talks. Both involved an exchange of land for peace.
In one, Ukraine would cede the “fortress belt” of cities in Donetsk and receive full NATO membership, the WSJ said.
But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected the idea of retreating from that well-defended position.
Russian official Dmitry Medvedev reiterated on November 20 that Ukraine’s potential NATO membership was a key reason for the war. He also suggested partitioning Ukraine, proposing that Lviv could be handed to Poland as part of a deal.
“The enemy has not abandoned its goal of destroying Ukrainian statehood,” said Ukraine’s Defence Ministry.
US negotiator Jared Kushner told a Berlin news conference that Russia had accepted a watered-down version of this US proposal – the second option outlined by the WSJ – of creating NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine in return for freezing the front line.
“We have been able to convince the Russians of this concept that any security guarantees for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” Kushner said. “President Trump is open to it, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest.”
It would be in the US interest, as he explained on social media, if “broader security arrangements made it highly unlikely that the guarantee would ever be invoked. This is why security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalised in isolation from post-war European security architecture.”
It appeared, therefore, that Europe would have to assume the burden of a future defence of Ukraine, something Russia has also rejected, because it refuses to accept European forces on Ukrainian soil.
Those NATO-style guarantees would have to be offered from the safety of NATO soil, rendering them less effective.
Zelenskyy told journalists he did not trust a deal between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom Trump referred to as “my friend” on November 19.
He told Bloomberg the US and Russia were effectively in cahoots to bully Ukraine.
“It’s very unfortunate when, during discussions about how to end the war, Starshield either malfunctions or has limitations, and not only are there fewer missiles for Patriot systems, but there are also other issues that prevent deliveries,” he said.
“Politically, it looks as if [the US] is moving in the same direction as what Putin wants: to force Ukraine into unfavourable compromises,” Zelenskyy said.
Europe did not appear to be in a listening mood any more than Ukraine.
“Russia wants more than Ukraine,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz told parliament. “Russia is escalating in the Baltic. Russia is escalating in Poland. Russia is escalating on the Black Sea. Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is escalating massively here in our own country.”
Merz was referring to two Russian missiles and a Russian drone, which crashed in an area of Poland on November 20, where a multinational force of more than 5,000 personnel from Britain, France, Belgium, Estonia, Spain, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Germany, Poland and Sweden was conducting its first military exercise.
Ukraine made its own response to Russia very clear during the past week.

items.text:
France is dealing with water insecurity – a new study shows it's a global problem
Tens of thousands of people in France are living under water restrictions as the country deals with a drought despite recent rains, according to the environment ministry. But this is a global problem, as a new study released Wednesday revealed "the largest global decline in surface water resources recorded" since 1991, when data collection began.
France has a water problem. An estimated 1.5 million people are affected by low water supply, and around 89,000 people are dealing with at least one type of emergency restriction, according to the country's environment ministry.
An estimated two-thirds of those 89,000 people are experiencing partial water cuts. In Creuse, a region in central France, officials last week deployed water trucks to fill up reserves and ensure water continued to flow through residents' taps.
Read moreEl Niño fuels climate disasters: The high price of inaction
Brittany is also "on the verge of collapse" when it comes to access to drinking water, Stéphane Roudaut, the mayor of Brest, a port city in the northwestern French region, reportedly told AFP in late October.
This comes as the country's geological institute reported earlier this month that two-thirds of the country's groundwater supplies are below their monthly average, despite some rain. The institute called these levels "extremely worrying".
France is not alone. A new study also published Wednesday has revealed that during record-breaking temperatures in 2023 and 2024, surface water levels, notably in rivers and lakes, declined at rates not recorded since 1991, when data collection began.
1.2 million lakes and reservoirs
The study, led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and including scientists from around the world, looked at water levels of some 150 river basins and around 1.2 million lakes and reservoirs.
“This is water that people and ecosystems directly depend on for drinking water, irrigation, hydropower, water transport and habitats for aquatic plants and animals,” Gia Destouni, a co-author of the study and professor in hydrology at Stockholm University, said.
The researchers found that between 2023 and 2024, global river flow fell around 5.7 percent below its average rate, and water in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5 percent.
Both 2023 and 2024 were the hottest years on record. The latter still holds the title, as 2025 fell just short of beating its high temperatures.
But 2026 is set to be the second-hottest year recorded, just after 2024, according to Europe's Copernicus programme.
Beyond water levels, these global temperatures had a real human cost. In France, more than 5,000 people died because of the heatwaves in 2023 and just under 4,000 excess deaths were recorded the following year. In Europe as a whole, more than 60,000 people died because of the 2024 summer heatwaves.
But Latin America was particularly affected by lowering water levels, according to the study published in the journal Science.
Latin America was worst hit because, at the time, the El Nino climate phenomenon caused the Pacific Ocean to heat up while the North Atlantic was also exceptionally warm – causing less rainfall, even in places that have historically been quite wet.
“What’s surprising is that not only traditionally dry regions were affected, but also the normally very rainy Amazon region,” said Gunter Bloschl, another senior author for the study and a researcher at the Institute of Hydraulic Engineering and Water Resources Management at TU Wien in Austria.
In 2024, this caused around 200 pink water dolphins to die in Brazil's Lake Tefe after water levels dropped to just 2 metres deep and 100 metres wide. Before this drop, heavy ferries and canoes could easily pass through its waters.
"Nobody thought this drought would come so quickly," Clodomar Lima, a fisherman in the region, told Reuters at the time.
"Water is everything to us. It is part of our daily lives, the means of transportation for everyone who lives here. Without water, we are nobody!" Francisco Alvaro Santos, a resident in the area, also told the news agency.
More rain over the ocean
More than two billion people globally lack access to safe drinking water, and 50 percent of the world's population is dealing with water scarcity, according to the United Nations.
These figures are only expected to rise as the climate crisis continues.
Bloschl also stressed this concern, saying one of the main takeaways from the report is "not about everything getting drier every year”, but whether irregularities in water supplies can increase insecurity.
The study found that between 2023 and 2024, precipitation actually increased over the ocean while it decreased over land.
“Global warming is changing not only evaporation, but also the large-scale distribution of water," Bloschl said. "As a result, droughts can be much more severe than one would expect based on warming alone. "
Like the Amazon, "regions that were previously considered water-rich can suddenly be affected by severe drought”.
Australia, like France, is also dealing with drought. According to TU Wien, where Bloschl is a researcher, from January to October 2026, "rainfall was around one-third less than the long-term average".
The period between August 2025 and July 2026 was also the driest since 1850. This dry period has seen lower groundwater levels and river flows.
“The large-scale atmospheric mechanisms in Austria are naturally different from those in the Amazon region,” Bloschl said.
“But the basic message is the same: Water availability depends not only on how much precipitation falls, but also on how much water evaporates, how much is stored in the ground, and how much ultimately reaches the rivers.”
In France, the country's weather monitoring agency, Météo-France, has reported that a wetter-than-normal scenario is likely in the coming months, especially in the northern part of the country.

Big EU defence projects under threat from proposed budget cuts: Commissioner Andrius Kubilius
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
We speak to the EU's Commissioner for Defence and Space, Andrius Kubilius. The former prime minister of Lithuania – who grew up during the Soviet era – tells us how he sees the confrontation between Europe and Russia. He also sounds the alarm over proposed cuts in the EU's future budget, saying that they could jeopardise major European projects in defence and space. Kubilius praises the EU's SAFE defence loans programme, remarking that it has been "really very successful".
Kubilius warns that cuts in the EU's next long-term budget, proposed by member states, could have serious consequences.
"We are definitely worried because we calculated very clearly (the funding for) projects that we need to develop in Europe, both in defence and space," he explains. "And we see that member states and leaders of institutions are proposing to cut our initial proposal by 30 percent, cutting down by €40 billion. This is one of the biggest cuts among all the spending lines of the next MFF (Multiannual Financial Framework). We are really concerned because there is the danger that European defence projects of common interest, or space projects like Iris Square or the Earth Observation Governmental Service (EOGS) – we shall not be able to implement them because of a lack of money at the European level."
Noting that "the space sector is now becoming very crucial for defence", Kubilius reacts to reports from Germany that Russia is considering launching a nuclear-armed satellite – something that Moscow denies.
"Nuclear weapons in space are very dangerous because they can totally destroy our space systems, which are crucial both for civilian life and for our security and defence," Kubilius says. "So we need to look at how we can defend our systems in space, also against the possibility of our adversaries trying to destroy them."
Kubilius believes that proposed EU budget cuts send the wrong signal at a time when Russia is rapidly increasing its own capabilities.
"Russia is increasing its defence-military budget up to €180 billion. That's 30 percent more than they spent this year," he notes. "And we cannot look only into nominal numbers because when we are comparing ourselves with Russia, we need to use the so-called purchasing power parity method of comparison. And then it appears that Russia next year will spend around €500, €550 billion. And this is the same amount or even a little bit more than the EU member states together. In addition to that, we see that Russian industry is able to produce more, and to innovate. This year Russia is producing around 10 million drones. Ukrainians are matching that number. But Ukrainians are predicting that Russians next year will be able to produce 20 million drones, and they will also increase their production of ballistic missiles."
Even if the EU and Ukraine are only just achieving parity with Russia, Kubilius credits the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme with playing an important part in boosting European defence. "It was really very successful," Kubilius states. "And now we have made a second call; we are asking member states to look into the possibility of taking those loans and using them to scale up production; European production, which is very much needed for Ukraine. We have an industrial challenge because when our industries present the contracts to Ukraine, the delivery dates are usually not 2027, but 2028 or 2029. So that is why we are trying to incentivise member states to scale up and to produce more quickly, and to do more for Ukrainian needs."

Almost every European teenager is online. Some 96 percent of 15-year-olds use social media, yet many say they do not feel safe there. One in four children in the EU, aged 12 to 17, report having experienced cyberbullying, and nearly one in three say social media has left them feeling stressed, sad or socially excluded.
Governments around the world are now asking whether more needs to be done to protect children online. Australia became the first country to ban social media for under-16s in 2025, while the European Union is considering its own response through the proposed EU Kids Act.
The legislation would create a child-specific framework for the digital world, covering everything from social media and video-sharing platforms to AI chatbots and online games. So will the EU Kids Act provide stronger protections for children without undermining young people's freedom of expression and access to information? We put the question to two MEPs.

items.title: France seeks German man in Channel migrant boat probe
items.summary:
Migrant deaths: France seeks German boat maker for 'manslaughter'
November 27, 2026
France has issued an arrest warrant for a German businessman as part of an investigation regarding the migrant deaths in the English Channel.
Joint investigation by several media outlets including French daily Le Mon
items.text:
Migrant deaths: France seeks German boat maker for 'manslaughter'
November 27, 2026
France has issued an arrest warrant for a German businessman as part of an investigation regarding the migrant deaths in the English Channel.
Joint investigation by several media outlets including French daily Le Monde and the BBC showed that Marvin R.* of MaRe Boote, managing director of a small firm in western German town Werne, is suspected of being one of the main suppliers of inflatable boats smugglers use to journey across the Channel.
According to the media reports, the 35-year-old businessman is accused of supplying smuggling gangs with inflatable boats, engines and life jackets worth hundreds of thousands of euros.
UK authorities estimated that boats or engines linked to MaRe Boote were responsible for three in every 10 detected crossings during the first four months of this year, the BBC and Le Monde reported.
Arrested and released in Germany
The prosecutor in the northern French city of Lille, Samuel Finielz, confirmed late on Thursday that "five people had been arrested and a German national was briefly detained in his country."
According to Finielz, this is part of the investigation about Channel crossings and sinkings since May last year.
The five others are now held in pre-trial detention and were suspected of offenses including "assisting illegal entry and residence as part of an organized criminal group, involuntary manslaughter, involuntary injury and endangering the lives of others," Finielz told the media.
Lille authorities in May issued an arrest warrant against "the German national implicated in this case," he said, on charges of manslaughter and endangering the lives of others.
Marvin R. was arrested and released by German authorities and now required to appear before a French court before January, the prosecutor added.
The BBC wrote that Marvin R. is contesting extradition to France. He can not be formally charged until he is extradited to France, it noted.
How many migrants cross the English Channel?
Migrants frequently cross the English Channel from France to the United Kingdom in small rubber dinghy boats. It is a dangerous journey as the Channel is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year and there have been many deaths.
*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges us to refrain from revealing the full names.

items.summary:
Divisions deepen between EU member states after tense budget summit
November 27, 2026
EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday nigh
items.text:
Divisions deepen between EU member states after tense budget summit
November 27, 2026
EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.
Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.
There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.
"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.
The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa.
Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."
Germany demands more for competitiveness, security, defense
Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.
Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."
As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.
In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).
"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."
Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.
"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.
Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.
Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.
They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.
In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.
EU looking elsewhere to raise funds
The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.
The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.
But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland, where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn have their European headquarters.
"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.
Protecting the EU's top triple-A rating
There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.
The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine Le Pen, the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.
EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."
Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.
"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."

items.title: Turkey summons Georgian envoy after football fans' pro-Palestine protest sparks clashes
items.summary:
Turkey summons Georgian envoy after football fans' pro-Palestine protest sparks clashes
Turkey summoned Georgia's ambassador on Friday over violence that broke out at ‌a Europa League match in Batumi ‌between the Turkish Besiktas and Israeli Hapoel Beer-Sheva teams, according to a foreign ministry s
items.text:
Turkey summons Georgian envoy after football fans' pro-Palestine protest sparks clashes
Turkey summoned Georgia's ambassador on Friday over violence that broke out at ‌a Europa League match in Batumi ‌between the Turkish Besiktas and Israeli Hapoel Beer-Sheva teams, according to a foreign ministry source. Clashes erupted after Besiktas fans unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during the match, sparking the diplomatic row.
Turkey on Friday summoned Georgia's ambassador in Ankara a day after violent clashes during a UEFA Europa League match between Besiktas and Israeli side Hapoel Beer-Sheva, a foreign ministry source said.
The incidents prompted Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan to call his Georgian counterpart, Maka Botchorishvili, on Thursday night.
"We conveyed our reaction to the serious incidents that occurred during Besiktas's UEFA Europa League match in Batumi and shared various pieces of evidence," the source said.
"We demanded a thorough investigation into all aspects of the incidents and that the necessary legal proceedings be initiated against those responsible for the disproportionate use of force against and intervention against our citizens," the source added.
UEFA has launched a probe into the incident.
'Revolt against the occupation'
Turkish football fans clashed with police in Batumi, temporarily halting the match, which had been moved from Istanbul over security concerns.
Images from the stadium showed Besiktas supporters displaying a banner reading "Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine", waving Palestinian flags and chanting anti-Israel slogans before police intervened.
Georgia's interior ministry on Thursday said in a statement that "three officers sustained various injuries as a result of the fans' violent actions", adding that 16 people were detained.
It said some supporters had hurled stadium seats at officers and denied reports that police had used force in response to the display of pro-Palestinian flags and banners.
"We categorically deny these reports and emphasise that the fans' violent actions and physical clashes with police began before the flags and banners were displayed, while they were still marching towards the stadium," the ministry added.
Police used pepper spray against fans, some of whom required medical attention, Turkey's private DHA news agency reported.
Detained Turkish fans released
The detained Turkish fans were released Friday, said the Georgian interior ministry. Turkey's state news agency Anadolu said President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had instructed Justice Minister Akin Gurlek to intervene to secure the release of 16 fans detained.
The match was suspended in the 26th minute because of disturbances in the stands, with Danish referee Morten Krogh sending both teams to the dressing rooms.
Turkey's football federation strongly condemned what it described as the "unacceptable" conduct of Georgian police towards Besiktas supporters.
"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the UEFA Europa League match," the federation said in a statement.
'Disproportionate use of force'
UEFA announced last month that the fixture would be moved to Georgia after Turkish authorities informed European football's governing body that, "for safety and security reasons", the match could not be hosted in Istanbul.
Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply since the outbreak of the Gaza war.
Erdogan, a staunch supporter of the Palestinian cause, has repeatedly accused Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza.
Read moreErdogan accuses Israel of 'genocide' over Gaza deaths
Pro-Palestinian banners and chants are seen or heard frequently at Turkish football matches, particularly since the start of the war.
Besiktas said they had lodged a complaint with UEFA over what they described as the "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
"We have launched initiatives with our consulate general in Batumi and UEFA regarding the disproportionate use of force against our supporters by security forces," the club said.
Erdogan spoke by phone with Besiktas chairman Serdal Adali and said he was closely following developments, the club said.
Messages of support
After the match, which finished 2-1 to Besiktas, Hapoel Beer-Sheva posted a message on social media directed to their travelling supporters.
"Please act responsibly, show restraint and use your best judgement as you leave the stadium and make your way to your accommodation. Follow the instructions of the Georgian security forces, who are responsible for ensuring your safety," the club posted in Hebrew on X.
Messages of support poured in on social media from across Turkey, including from the sports minister and Ankara mayor.
Even Besiktas's traditional Istanbul rivals, Galatasaray and Fenerbahce, as well as Black Sea club Trabzonspor, condemned the incidents and expressed solidarity with the club.
A Besiktas club employee told AFP that five supporters received treatment in hospital.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

A few weeks ago, Alessio Dionisi was forced to deny the “fake news” he had joined Sean Dyche, Gianfranco Zola, Beppe Sannino, Óscar García, Billy McKinlay, Slavisa Jokanovic, Quique Sánchez Flores (twice), Walter Mazzarri, Marco Silva, Javi Gracia (twice), Nigel Pearson, Vladimir Ivic
items.text:
HELLO, GOODBYE
A few weeks ago, Alessio Dionisi was forced to deny the “fake news” he had joined Sean Dyche, Gianfranco Zola, Beppe Sannino, Óscar García, Billy McKinlay, Slavisa Jokanovic, Quique Sánchez Flores (twice), Walter Mazzarri, Marco Silva, Javi Gracia (twice), Nigel Pearson, Vladimir Ivic, Xisco Muñoz, Claudio Ranieri, Roy Hodgson, Rob Edwards, Slaven Bilic, Chris Wilder, Valérien Ismael, Tom Cleverley, Paulo Pezzolano and Edward Still in being sacked by the Pozzo family since 2012. There was no denial on Sunday, when the axe inevitably fell on the head coach following a 4-0 shellacking at Sheffield United and the Italian left after only 18 games in charge. While his reign is unlikely to live long in the memory of anyone at Vicarage Road, Dionisi can at least boast on his LinkedIn page that in terms of longevity under the Pozzos, he took charge of 18 more matches than Dyche, 17 more than García and 16 more than McKinlay. Indeed, he even outlasted Rob Edwards, who was assured he would be backed “come hell or high water” upon his 2022 appointment, only to be fired from the ejector seat 11 games later.
It’s been quite the white-knuckle ride for Watford since the Pozzos arrived, armed only with a spreadsheet, an army of Udinese cast-offs and knowledge of the loophole that there was no Football League cap on the number of players who could be brought in on loan from clubs outside the UK. And while few fans will be able to recall all 25 of the coaches who have been hired and fired by the Pozzos, they do have fond memories to take to the grave. There was that end-to-end Troy Deeney play-off semi-final goal against Leicester. There were five uninterrupted seasons in the Premier League. There was that time they ended Liverpool’s 44-match unbeaten Premier League run despite being stuck in the relegation zone. And what self-respecting Hornet will ever forget travelling to watch their team play in the 2019 FA Cup final?
Of course it hasn’t all been rosy in the Pozzo garden. The eight-day managerial reign of McKinlay was a source of much mirth for fans of rival clubs. A double relegation from the Premier League – the first amid allegations of a dressing-room bust-up linked to an illegal lockdown party – wasn’t great either. Playing I’m Still Standing by Elton John, the club’s honorary life president, over the Vicarage Road PA system to mark their descent into the Championship heaped further embarrassment upon the club. And what self-respecting Hornet will ever forget travelling home after watching their team play in the 2019 FA Cup final?
While it would be foolish to predict what will happen next at a club that currently sit two places above the Championship relegation zone, the one stonewall certainty is that the name “Edward Iordanescu” will be the next to be copied and pasted into the over-worked club template announcing a managerial departure. The Romanian was formally introduced this morning and with this being his 14th job in the past 16 years, he can arguably lay claim to being the most ‘Watford’ manager of the Pozzo era. “For me, I want a team that plays very good, organised football with the spirit and attitude, and the strong mentality,” he blathered, as local reporters dabbed their bingo cards. “And then, yes, regarding the organisation of the team, that takes time.” History suggests getting the time he needs is a pipe dream for Iordanescu, whose first game in charge is away at Championship basement-dwellers Derby County. Should Watford go to Pride Park and lose, he could be out of a job by Saturday night.

QUOTE OF THE DAY
“I know people expect me to say: ‘Oh, I regret it.’ No, I don’t regret it. If I regret something, it’s that I would love to kick him in another [place]. The kung fu kick was criticised a lot, especially by journalists. But now it’s a [more positive] symbol. So I change everything” – Eric Cantona is in scintillating form during this chat with Donald McRae.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 
 If you’ve never tried listening to or watching the utter drivel that is ‘The Overlap’, this will mean nothing whatsoever, but if you have, this, by the great Jonathan Liew, is absolutely superb. Satire so biting it even surpasses Luis Suárez at his 2010, 2013 and 2014 peaks” – Noble Francis.
 
 I read your depressing piece about Burnley (yesterday’s Football Daily, full email edition). I am in the unfortunate position of being a season ticket holder at Turf Moor and residing in south-east London. A typical Saturday home game starts for me at 6am, involves two train journeys, the underground and a bus ride (that’s each way) getting home about midnight. Then there is the travel and food costs which are usually in the three figures. Evening games, like Wednesday, involve two days and a friend’s spare room. As a 70-year-old is it too much to expect a similar effort from those overpaid prancing show ponies that think they are too good for Burnley, too good for the Championship – if it’s only just for two hours on match day? There, I’ve said it and I feel much better. That is , of course, until 5pm on Saturday” – Chris Harrison.

Gadi Eisenkot has accused the Likud party of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of stalling coalition t
items.text:
Israel’s Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu’s party of stalling coalition talks
Yahsar party chief says Netanyahu’s Likud wants to drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government.
Gadi Eisenkot has accused the Likud party of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of stalling coalition talks in a bid to bring about new elections.
Following the October 27 election, the leader of the centrist Yashar party has been tapped by Israel’s president to form a new government but has so far struggled to put together a ruling coalition.
He has until December 6 to form a government to replace Netanyahu. The deadline can be extended by 14 days.
The election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc. Eisenkot and his presumed partners won 48 seats, well short of a majority in the 120-seat parliament.
Netanyahu and his traditional alliance of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties won 53 seats, also short of a majority.
The Yashar party has so far agreed coalition deals with the left-leaning Democrats party and the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party.
Together, they have a combined total of 36 MPs – still short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority.
National unity government
Yashar negotiators have also held talks with Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party over the possibility of forming a national unity government involving both parties – without any breakthrough.
“Likud, for its part, was unwilling to compromise and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table,” Eisenkot said in a statement on Friday.
“Their conduct points to an effort to run down the clock until the mandate expires, split the Change bloc and drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government,” he added.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging camp has faced divisions on whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox parties or the Arab-majority lists, or whether to form a unity government with Likud.
“We are approaching a moment of decision,” Eisenkot said.
“The question is whether Likud will engage in serious negotiations and commit to a partnership that requires compromise or keep up appearances and continue to stall,” he added, while maintaining that he was still open to talks if Likud was “genuinely prepared to change course”.
Likud accused Eisenkot of working to form a “dangerous left-wing government” but nonetheless said it would still be open to a unity government.

items.text:
Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy, halts flights and ticket sales
Passengers advised to seek refunds via bankruptcy process, though guarantees are not assured, warns Norse Atlantic.
Norwegian budget airline Norse Atlantic said it would file for bankruptcy for its main Norwegian operating unit and has stopped selling tickets, becoming the latest airline casualty of fuel-cost spikes stemming from the war in Iran..
The airline has cancelled all flights and said on its website that its customer service department is no longer available.
The shutdown came quickly. On Wednesday, the airline, which was founded in 2021, said its financial situation was “critical”. A day later, it suspended flights and warned that it could file for bankruptcy if it failed to secure funding.
By Friday, the airline said it could not raise the money it needed to continue flying.
Norse is the latest airline to struggle with rising fuel costs brought on by the US-led war in Iran. Latvia’s airBaltic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September, while US budget airline Spirit Airlines went out of business in May.
Jet fuel prices have risen 71 percent globally over the past year and more than 78 percent in Europe, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA) which tracks jet fuel prices.
“We were unable to absorb the extra cost … Fuel is what toppled this company,” CEO Eivind Roald told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.
Norse said on its website that passengers could seek refunds through the bankruptcy process but warned that refunds were not guaranteed. It advised customers to check their travel insurance or contact their banks.
“This is a very hard day for the pilots and their families, and for all other Norse employees. Our thoughts are also with the passengers whose journeys are now cancelled,” the board of the Norse Atlantic Pilots Association told the Reuters news agency.
The airline also began ending its aircraft leasing agreements with AerCap Holdings and BOC Aviation, which were for 12 and 16 years, respectively.
Norse’s shares fell nearly 69 percent on the Oslo Stock Exchange on Friday, bringing its losses this year to 99.86 percent. In the US, its shares fell 85 percent on Friday, trading at a fraction of a cent.

items.summary:
Brussels' most anticipated new museum opens its doors
November 27, 2026
Brussels is best known as the de facto capital of the European Union. But beyond its role as a political hub, it also boasts a thriving contemporary art scene.
Yet the Belgian city didn't have a major museum of modern and contem
items.text:
Brussels' most anticipated new museum opens its doors
November 27, 2026
Brussels is best known as the de facto capital of the European Union. But beyond its role as a political hub, it also boasts a thriving contemporary art scene.
Yet the Belgian city didn't have a major museum of modern and contemporary art on the scale of Paris' Pompidou or London's Tate Modern. This now changes with the opening of Kanal-Centre Pompidou on November 28.
The museum aims to "make Brussels a world-class cultural destination," on par with the Guggenheim in Bilbao or the MoMA in New York, Boris Dillies, the head of the regional government, told press agency AFP.
Behind this new museum is an ambitious architectural project involving the transformation of a vast industrial landmark into a multidisciplinary cultural institution.
A modern art museum inside a car factory
Instead of building the new museum from scratch, Kanal was designed to occupy the former Citroën garage and factory complex, built in 1933-34 beside the Brussels canal.
Originally standing as a symbol of modernity and industrial progress, the factory was a space where cars were serviced and assembled, as well as displayed. The former Citroën showroom now serves as a glass-and-steel space that rises 21 meters high.
Rather than erasing the building's industrial past, the project's architects — noAarchitecten, EM2N and Sergison Bates, working together as Atelier Kanal — decided to celebrate its original structures. Vast concrete volumes and industrial details remain visible, creating a dialogue between the site's history and its new cultural purpose.
Like London's Tate Modern, which transformed a power station into a museum, Kanal shows how industrial architecture can gain a second life without losing its identity.
"Kanal reveals how architecture can reinvent the museum typology, not only as a place for art, but as a stage for the city and its citizens," Atelier Kanal said in a statement, adding that their concept for the former Citroën factory ensured that the space would be "renewed without being erased, made precise without being overdetermined and open to continued transformation."
Covering around 40,000 square meters, the complex is one of the largest cultural buildings in Belgium.
The Pompidou connection
Kanal has established a partnership agreement with the Centre Pompidou in Paris that has guided both the international outlook of the new museum, as well as its intention to remain rooted in Brussels' local culture.
"A place for all people" was the founding vision of the Centre Pompidou, articulated by its architects Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano as they designed the iconic institution in the 1970s.
Kanal's collaboration with the Centre Pompidou, which runs until 2031, gives the Brussels museum access to one of the world's greatest collections of modern and contemporary art. Visitors will be able to see works that normally reside in Paris, while also encountering pieces from Belgian collections and newly commissioned projects.
The Brussels museum has already announced some of the upcoming exhibitions that will be drawing from the Pompidou's collection during their five-year partnership: two photography exhibitions focusing on Robert Frank and Brassaï, as well as art exhibitions focusing on iconic figures of modernism: Robert and Sonia Delaunay, Braque, Picasso and Matisse.
The new institution however emphasizes that it is not a branch of the Pompidou. The partnership is rather envisioned as a dialogue between two museums with different perspectives and histories.
The Centre Pompidou itself has been closed for major renovations since September 2025, and is scheduled to reopen in 2030.
10 opening exhibitions
The headline exhibition, "A truly immense journey," brings together more than 350 works from the collections of Centre Pompidou, Kanal and numerous Belgian lenders, and will feature modern icons including Lygia Clark, Sonia Delaunay, Alberto Giacometti, Natalia Goncharova, Wifredo Lam and Henri Matisse.
Along with this show, nine other exhibitions fill the building.
One of them, "An infinite woman," focuses on how mass-produced image of a Mangbetu woman long served as a colonial symbol and how artists of African descent have reappropriated and subverted this imagery.
Another one, "Right to the City — Right to the Future," explores the architectural transformation of the Brussels' Quartier Nord, which was historically a working-class neighborhood that was largely cleared in the 1960s to become a high-rise business district — displacing over 15,000 residents.
The museum as a third space
Alongside modern and contemporary art, Kanal is dedicated to architecture, landscape and the performing arts.
This reflects a broader shift in the role of museums, which are increasingly expected to be places where people gather, exchange ideas and engage with contemporary issues rather than simply admire objects behind glass.
The opening program alone demonstrates the museum's ambitions, offering a 36-hour non-stop program of live performances, opening rituals, concerts, DJ sets, films, installations and workshops for children and families, with events open to everyone.
The exhibitions can also be visited for free during the inaugural weekend. Visitors however need to have previously booked a time slot; all 30,000 tickets were snapped up within 24 hours of their release.
Edited by: Sarah Hucal

Saturday tips: Kap Vert fancied to lift Coral Gold Cup crown at Newbury
Wendigo heads the market for a typically competitive renewal of the Coral Gold Cup at Newbury, with Mr Hope Street, Road To Home and Kap Vert among the challengers; Panic Attack back to defend her crown for in-form Dan Skelton team
Friday 27 November 2026 16:28, UK
With a hugely exciting renewal of the Coral Gold Cup on Saturday, Kate Tracey, Declan Rix and Sam Boswell headed to Newbury for a very special episode of Weekend Winners.
The familiar trio have each had a close look at the famous handicap clash as well as a brilliant supporting card, all live on Sky Sports Racing from 11am.
Jamie Snowden's Wendigo is the pre-race favourite and promises to bring the house down if scoring for the well-supported Racing Club syndicate, while last year's winner Panic Attack returns with 10lb claimer Dominic Lewis on board for the in-form Dan Skelton team.
- Newbury's Coral Gold Cup: Jamie Lynch's horse-by-horse guide
- Three for the Coral Gold Cup! Sean Boyce's Newbury preview
At The Races' Declan Rix…
"My horse is Kap Vert. He's only a six-year-old but for a novice to go and win the Scottish National I thought was a big effort.
"All he's done is progress and improve. This horse's big asset is his jumping and he's got a prominent style of racing, which I like for the track.
"If the rain does come, we know he's going to handle that and it puts more emphasis on his stamina.
"It's a big ride for Sean Houlihan and if he can bounce him out early and get into a rhythm, his jumping will keep him in it."
Host Kate Tracey…
"I don't want too much rain to come down for my pick: Miami Magic.
"He had the perfect prep for this, in my opinion, in a Pertemps Qualifier here on November 5.
"It didn't exactly go to plan early on in his chasing career but I think he's got his act together now.
"I'm hoping it will be fair ground for him to bounce off."
BetVictor's Sam Boswell…
"It's unoriginal, but I'm with Wendigo. It's competitive from a betting angle but I think it looks a little bit shy of real top-class future chasers.
"This is the one horse who could maybe be that and he's 40/1 for the Grand National.
"The trip is the one thing people might throw at him because he's an old-fashioned chaser who needs a bit of getting after but once he does, he'll stay on really nicely.
"For me, he's the standout. He's a really strong and obvious contender. For Jamie Snowden and the Lambourn trainers, this is their Cheltenham Gold Cup. This is a special race and I think it will go to a local trainer."

items.summary:
Trump backs Iraqi PM’s oil smuggling crackdown
Baghdad closes border crossings as Kurdish authorities warn of constitutional violations and call for meeting.
US President Donald Trump has backed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s drive to stop oil smuggling and assert state authority, moves that ha
items.text:
Trump backs Iraqi PM’s oil smuggling crackdown
Baghdad closes border crossings as Kurdish authorities warn of constitutional violations and call for meeting.
US President Donald Trump has backed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s drive to stop oil smuggling and assert state authority, moves that have put Baghdad in direct confrontation with Kurdish authorities and Iran-aligned militias.
Trump said in a Truth Social post on Friday that Washington supports al-Zaidi’s efforts to “stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state”.
He said the United States wants a “united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions”. The endorsement comes as al-Zaidi, who has steered Iraq closer to Washington, risks antagonising both the Kurds and Iran, Agence France-Presse reported.
Haider al-Aboudi told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that Baghdad considers crude exports bypassing state marketer SOMO to be smuggling, since the proceeds do not reach the treasury. He said Iraq lost an estimated $100bn to smuggling through northern Iraq’s Kurdish region between 2008 and 2025.
Reuters said it was unclear how the government calculated the figure.
On Tuesday, al-Zaidi moved to place the Kurdish region’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control, AFP reported. Iraq closed two crossings in the region on Thursday, one with Syria and one with Iran. Iraq’s highest court ruled on Wednesday that Baghdad can deploy federal forces along all international borders, including those of the Kurdish region of northern Iraq.
Oil Minister Basim Mohammed said: “The oilfields in the region and Basra belong to all Iraqis and remain under the Iraqi flag.” INA reported that he said Iraq would not be lenient towards “any drop of oil exported outside legal contexts”.
Kurdish reaction
Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) spokesman Peshawa Hawramani said the region does not want clashes with Baghdad, but sees the central government’s actions as aimed at restricting the semi-autonomous region and violating its constitutional rights.
“We are not in favour of clashes and disagreement, but that does not mean we accept the violation of Kurdistan’s rights guaranteed by the constitution,” he said.
The Kurdish government on Wednesday rejected the “military language and threats” in a statement from the Iraqi military spokesman, Reuters reported. It said it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption. Thousands of Kurds protested the decision on Thursday.
The Kurdish crackdown came a week after al-Zaidi ordered the army to prepare to enter Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad, where the government accuses the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah of running a smuggling operation.
Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdelwahed, reporting from Erbil, said residents fear for their livelihoods if Baghdad takes over the region’s oil infrastructure, and spoke of a “trust deficiency” between the two governments. He said the Kurdish government denies any illicit oil operations and calls the campaign an attempt to undermine Kurdish constitutional and territorial rights.
A meeting sponsored by the head of the Supreme Judicial Council is set for December 1 in Baghdad, he said. If it fails or stalls, the sides could face a constitutional and political conflict.
Why it matters
Sajad Jiyad, an analyst at the Center for International Policy, told AFP that al-Zaidi’s “strategy is aligned with what America wants for Iraq and for its Iran policy”. Cutting off the oil flow, he said, is “exactly what US policy is right now: maximum pressure through economic blockade”.
Trump has welcomed al-Zaidi at the White House, where he called him “a great fighter” and “a great fan of America”.

items.title: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec law barring public sector workers from wearing religious symbols
items.summary: Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those right
items.text:
Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.
In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning, the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.
“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” chief justice Richard Wagner wrote in the majority opinion.
Canada’s top court says the four days of hearings from earlier in the year marked one of the longest in its 151-year history. Fifty-one interveners participated, including six attorneys general – also a record number. The court’s website crashed on Friday morning when the judgment was released.
While the judgment was celebrated by some in Quebec who considered it a vindication of the province’s fight, it was swiftly criticised by religious civil liberties groups.
“We cannot exist in a country as free people, where governments can literally go to the electorate and say, ‘I’m gonna take away the rights of a certain group of minorities’, because it’s popular and to play wedge politics with the charter rights of Canadians,” Stephen Brown, chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, told reporters at a press conference. “If that is the case, we don’t have a charter of rights and freedoms. We have a charter of suggestions and permissions.”
Passed in 2019, Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, bars workers including lawyers, judges, police and teachers from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah or a cross while on the job.
Central to the case – and the reason provincial governments across the country are closely watching the result – is the “notwithstanding clause”, a constitutional mechanism that allows elected governments to override certain fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The clause is the result of political compromise from the 1980s, when the federal government set out to replace the existing British North America Act with a new constitution. Provinces feared that under a new constitution, courts would become too powerful, undermining the authority of the elected government. A compromise was hashed out: in cases when a government – provincial or federal – felt that the courts had overstepped, they could invoke the clause to override certain charter rights of citizens.
Some fundamental rights, including protections of religious freedom, equality and speech, could be suspended. But voting, as well as language rights, were untouchable, ensuring Canadians could remove a government if they wanted. A government could only invoke the clause for five years. Before they could renew it, they would first have to face voters.
In its decision, the supreme court rejected most arguments that Bill 21 violated portions of the charter that are not subject to the notwithstanding clause, including guarantees relating to the equality of men and women and the education rights of Quebec’s English-speaking minority.
Quebec’s use of the clause with Bill 21 was notable – and controversial – in that it was the first time the notwithstanding clause had been invoked pre-emptively in an attempt to shield the law from court challenges. Quebec also passed Bill 96, which sought to strengthen French language protections – again pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause.
But groups affected by those laws can still challenge them and many teachers, religious and civil liberties groups argued it was a clear violation of constitutional rights and reflected government overreach. Quebec’s government has defended the law, saying it is constitutionally valid.
In April 2021, a Quebec superior court judge described the effects of the law as “cruel”, saying it “dehumanises” the people it targets, but conceded the statute could not be struck down because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s court of appeal also upheld the law in February 2024 on the same grounds.
In its 520-page judgment, the court did find that element of the law infringed on democratic rights protected by the charter, including preventing elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly who wear face coverings for religious reasons from participating in the legislative process.
In a 4-3 decision, the court also endorsed the ability of lower courts to issue “judicial declarations” on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause, giving judges the power to declare a law in violation of the charter, even though the law would be permitted to stand.
The court’s decision was celebrated in Quebec, where the governing Parti Québécois has looked for wedges with the federal government and institutions like the supreme court.
The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, had previously said his province’s right to decide its own laws was at risk.
Canada only recently fended off a threat to national unity after voters in Alberta rejected the initial stages of a separatist push. But Quebec’s newly elected government has shown an eagerness to clash with the prime minister, Mark Carney.
The supreme court’s judgment comes on the same day an appeal will be heard regarding a superior court decision that forces Quebec’s members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to King Charles to sit in the Salon Bleu – the chamber of the assembly. Lawmakers from a number of parties in the province recently refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

items.text:
Serbia's Student List runs chemistry professor for president
November 27, 2026
A long-time supporter of the Serbian student movement, chemistry professor and researcher Radomir Saicic, is set to run for president on behalf of the Student List in late December.
Saicic accepted the nomination on Friday, a day after Serbia's new parliament scheduled the ballot for December 27.
In his acceptance speech, the Belgrade University lecturer said state institutions, including its president, needed to "win back public trust."
"It's time to restore dignity to the office of Serbian president," he said.
"Once we can agree with each other about things that matter to all of us despite our differences, Serbia will have the strength to decide its future on its own, and to have its voice heard and respected in the world," he added.
Vucic barred from running again
The 65-year-old is one of the lawmakers in the new assembly, which was formed in the wake of the Student List ousting the regime of Serbia's longtime strongman ruler Aleksandar Vucic at the parliamentary polls last month.
Vucic is banned by the constitution from running for president after winning two terms. He has hinted at his party boycotting the presidential vote.
While the office of the Serbian president is officially far less powerful that the office of Serbian prime minister, Vucic managed to organize his rule around himself during his time as prime minister and then hold on to levers of power while serving as president.
Saicic sees Kosovo as 'occupied territory'
On Friday, Saicic accused the "outgoing regime" of "still trying to collapse our state."
"This past decade was marred by the breakdown of the rule of law, corruption, and hate speech," he said.
Saicic, a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Art, is seen by many as a moderate nationalist and a traditionalist.
He has notably described the neigboring, Albanian-dominated Kosovo, as "temporarily occupied territory," keeping in line with Belgrade's long-running policy of treating Kosovo as a breakaway province.
The presidential candidate has also urged a "productive relationship" with Russia, pointing to Serbia's energy needs.
Saicic pledges humility with Bible quote
While seemingly reticent on the topic of the European Union, Saicic told reporters on Friday that he has a "fundamentally positive stance toward Europe and European values," pointing to examples including environment protection, academic education, the rule of law, science and technological progress.
"All of these things we should develop as much as possible, not for the sake of meeting some formal criteria, but to actually be what we are supposed to be," he said.
Saicic has sought to present himself as a devout Orthodox Christian while simultaneously criticizing the Serbian church leaders for aligning with the Vucic regime.
In his Friday speech, Saicic quoted the Bible, saying that "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant."

items.text:
Spurs' Savio to miss festive fixtures after injury setback
- Published
Tottenham winger Savio will miss the club's Christmas fixtures with injury and could be out for up to 80 days, manager Roberto de Zerbi has confirmed.
Savio joined Spurs from Manchester City for £75m this summer, but has played in just five of their 11 Premier League matches this season.
The 22-year-old came on as a substitute in the 64th minute of Tottenham's 2-0 win over Ipswich on Saturday, but was forced off with two minutes remaining with a hamstring injury.
It was the attacker's first game back in six weeks after returning from a muscle problem which led to him missing the four previous league matches.
Asked if Savio, previously known as Savinho, would miss the Christmas schedule, De Zerbi said: "Yes, I think so unfortunately.
"It is a tough situation to accept. He is a good guy. He is suffering for this new injury but it is part of football."
"If you see the other European clubs, all of them, they are suffering many, many injuries."
Savio is still searching for his first league goal or assist for Tottenham, although he did score and assist a goal on his debut in August in a 5-1 win over Charlton in the Carabao Cup.
"Now, he needs time and hard work with the medical staff," De Zerbi added.
"Then in 50, 60 or 80 days - I don't know when he comes back - he'll be crucial for us for the last step of the season."
Tottenham are 10th in the league and have won four of their past five matches after a poor start to the season.
They travel to 18th-placed Sunderland on Sunday (14:05 GMT).

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU r
items.text:
Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
- Published
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".
France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.
In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".
Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat and poultry owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.
In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.
Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.
"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.
Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".
Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".
Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

items.text:
Netherlands: Authorities seize 26 rare turtles in luggage at Schiphol
November 27, 2026
The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday that it had seized more than two dozen critically endangered turtles that customs officers found in a passenger's luggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport.
The Vallarta mud turtles discovered in the luggage of a man flying to Hong Kong via Schiphol are endemic to Mexico. They were only formally discovered and catalogued in 2018 and are one of the smallest of all known genuses of turtle.
"These highly rare and protected turtles were presumably taken from the wild in Mexico, where an estimated population of only about 300 of these animals remain," the NVWA said in a press release.
How were the turtles discovered and smuggled?
Dutch customs agents discovered the animals on November 21 during a regular inspection and then alerted the NVWA, as the responsible agency for such cases, on realizing that they had uncovered live fauna.
Police then arrested the man at the NVWA's request, and the NVWA said in Friday's statement that he was still in custody, with federal prosecutors continuing their investigations.
"Most of the turtles were packed in a box alongside a toy car, while others were placed inside a sealed sock within a suitcase," the NVWA wrote. "The animals had been wrapped in duct tape, which prevented them from moving. All of the turtles survived the journey."
Authorities said the turtles were being housed at a specialized rescue facility, "where the duct tape was carefully removed," and where they were "receiving the care they require."
What are Vallarta mud turtles?
Vallarta mud turtles are exceptionally small freshwater turtles that only entered the taxonomical record in 2018, endemic to a very small area in western Mexico.
Relatively little is known about the creature owing both to its recent discovery and the damage to its habitat caused by urbanization and a growing tourist trade in the Mexican state of Jalisco.
The Turtle Island organization in Graz, Austria — which recently started breeding the turtles in Austria as a "genetic reservoir for eventual rewilding" and is working to help preserve them in Mexico — considers it "the world's smallest turtle species," and estimates that "over 99%" of its natural habitat has been lost to urbanization.
Roads and traffic are a particular risk for the slow-moving creatures.
"Despite strict protections, their small size and striking appearance make them prime targets for illegal collectors," Turtle Island says when detailing other risks to the tiny animals, that are not known to grow larger than 10 centimeters (less than 4 inches) in length.
The IUCN Red List classifies it as "Critically Endangered" and it is subject to the highest level of protection under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).
"The suspected poaching of 26 of these turtles from the wild may have reduced the population by nearly 10%," the NVWA wrote, basing its figure on the estimated population of around 300 of the turtles in the wild.
The agency urged people to report any suspected instances of illegal trade of protected animal or plant species, whether "via online forums, marketplaces, bird fairs, or antique and curiosity markets."
