items.text:
Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50m last summer.
On one level it looks like good business. Delap’s only season at Stamford Bridge featured one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one ridiculous red card and not much else. Analysts at other clubs rated him at Ipswich and felt Chelsea was the wrong fit for his direct style of play. The mistake was less the decision not to give Delap another season, no matter the worries over cover for João Pedro, more the call to sign him in the first place.
At the same time, however, Delap’s experience speaks to the questions around culture and identity dogging Chelsea before they face Forest and their former striker at the City Ground on Friday night. It is a point that could be applied to so many of the players to join during this ownership’s four years in charge. Alejandro Garnacho, languishing on loan at Aston Villa, was a £40m signing last year, and only three of the 12 players who joined in the 2024-25 season are still at the club.
There is a constant churn. Laurence Stewart has departed the five-strong sporting director team and there also are whispers around Dave Fallows, although insiders insist there will be no further changes. Back to the squad and Moisés Caicedo, Roméo Lavia and Cole Palmer are the only survivors from the 2023-24 intake. Wesley Fofana, Malo Gusto and Gaga Slonina remain from the 16 who joined in the 2022-23 season. The trading is relentless and, although the ability to raise funds meant Chelsea were in position to spend £117m on Morgan Rogers last summer, it is hard not to wonder whether the strategy has hindered the team’s development.
The lack of consistency was evident when Chelsea lost 4-1 at home to Leeds last Saturday. Xabi Alonso, whose side are eighth after five defeats in their first 11 league games, has focused on raising standards. But shifting mindset is harder when the players cannot fall back on a clear identity. The chopping and changing has consequences. Reece James, Chelsea’s captain, is the only first-teamer who represented the club during the Roman Abramovich era. It is not a surprise that supporters feel little connection to the players. Fans wonder whether the long contracts handed out to players have meaning. They hear Fofana appear to joke about missing a penalty against Liverpool and wonder whether the players care. It explains why the atmosphere at Stamford Bridge quickly grows toxic. The culture has to change. There has to be more accountability.
“This is a goal for us – that we are able to have stability, to be more competitive,” Alonso said on Thursday. “For me, to build that core, to build that way of doing things, it’s very important for the newcomers when you really get into the place and you know how things work.”
It is a work in progress. The final whistle against Leeds brought the sight of Palmer, who is horribly out of form, arguing with João Pedro and Willie Isa, the player support and development officer, about refusing to acknowledge the fans. There has been more woe this week, the mood soured by Fofana’s ill-advised chat with a French YouTuber. Fofana has had to apologise after failing to seek club permission for an interview in which he revealed that he almost quit football before his agents pointed out how much money was left on his contract.
Alonso, who refused to say whether the £75m defender had been fined, was unamused. “He apologised,” the manager said. “He knows it was not right. We are here to take things seriously.”
The worry is that Chelsea still look unserious. They have plenty to prove after being bullied by Leeds and Sunderland. Delap, who has been finetuning his heading in training this week, will fancy his chances after Fofana and Levi Colwill toiled against target men when they faced Leeds’ Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey.
Confidence in the defence is at rock bottom. Chelsea are not in Europe but Alonso is yet to feel the benefit of extra time on the training ground. His side have conceded 20 goals and keep making silly errors. Jamie Carragher, Alonso’s former teammate at Liverpool, destroyed the pairing of Fofana and Colwill on Sky Sports on this week’s Monday Night Football. They have been exposed by Maxence Lacroix’s hamstring injury. Alonso needs individuals to stop hiding. Chelsea’s midfield crumbled when Caicedo went off injured against Leeds, and the attack has spluttered without João Pedro.
There is no point crying about injuries. Chelsea have spent more than £1bn on their squad. Alonso, who accused his players of failing to perform the basics against Leeds, is yet to make sense of it all and has not instilled a playing identity. He talks about control but it is not clear what he wants Chelsea to be. It is Alonso’s puzzle to solve. Working it out will be easier if Chelsea finally develop some continuity.

items.text:
Hull City should be in League One this season according to Expected Goals - so how do the Tigers keep winning in the Premier League?
Hull City are sitting comfortably in the middle of the Premier League table - when the Expected Goals underlying data says they should be two divisions below; watch Crystal Palace vs Hull live on Sky Sports this Sunday from 1pm, kick-off 2pm
Thursday 26 November 2026 14:53, UK
Hull aren't doing much wrong as a newly promoted club so far. A great start to the campaign has them middle of the Premier League table, clear of the relegation zone and unbeaten at home all season.
These are all the right ingredients for survival. But the underlying data says otherwise.
If Expected Goals (xG) decided football matches - yes, yes, we know they don't - then Hull would be bottom of the Premier League, with a similar record to the actual bottom club Crystal Palace, who they play live on Sky Sports this Sunday.
The reason? Hull have only won one game this season on xG since their promotion to the top flight.On its own, this underlying data should be taken with a pinch of salt. xG numbers in a match require context.
For example, a team that loses a game can often end up having a higher xG than the opponent, as they were chasing the game and attacking for longer periods.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Hull news & transfers
- Hull fixtures & scores | FREE Hull highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
The same xG table also has Chelsea in 14th place at the moment. Bournemouth should be third and Nottingham Forest should be sixth. After 11 games, there is a lot of differentiation between the Expected Table and the actual table across the board.
But this isn't a new phenomenon when it comes to Hull. The fascinating thing about the Tigers is that this has been happening for 18 months.
The same xG data says Hull should also be playing in League One this season. That's because last term, they should have finished second-bottom of the Championship after 46 games, according to xG. Instead, they were promoted to the Premier League via the play-offs.
As Aston Villa showed last season, you can get away with overperforming this way for some time but things eventually regress to the mean. To do this over a long period of time is extraordinary.
So why are Hull where they are? Style has something to do with it.
Set up in a 5-4-1 formation, Hull have the lowest possession in the Premier League this season by an absolute country mile. The same applies for the number of shots they have and how high they start pressing up the pitch.
"It is not about possession, it is what you do with it," said manager Sergej Jakirovic told Sky Sports in an interview last month. Hull are comfortable in a low block, which ultimately leads to losing the 'stats side' of games.
So how do Hull actually win games? As their manager says, in the little time Hull get hold of the ball, they use it to good effect - the Tigers move the ball up the pitch quicker than any other team.
There is also an efficiency in attack. In the Championship last season, Hull had two of the most clinical forwards in Ollie McBurnie and Joe Gelhardt. They were given few opportunities, but when they got them, they took them.
The same culture applies here. "No matter who is the opponent, we will have our chances," added Jakirovic.
The aim of the game is not only to progress the ball as quickly as possible, but also choosing the right battles. That can be seen in Hull's pressing.
Hull barely press - they have the lowest number of high turnovers in the Premier League this season. However, they have the second-most goals from high turnovers this season and rank fourth for high pressures that end up in a shot. It's a selective, patient press.
Take their recent draw with Brentford as an example. Their only chance of the first half came from Hull pressing out-of-position midfielder Aaron Hickey to win a penalty which they scored from. Then they relied on the defence to hold out for a result. They conceded late, but got what many would say is a good point.
But this game plan of little possession and reliance on taking advantage of the few attacks that come their way is risky. You need a lot of luck to go your way, and Hull have had their fair share of that.
In the Championship last season, Hull had the most let-offs out of any second-tier team in terms of big chances missed by their opponents. A similar theme has continued in the Premier League.
In Hull's first two home games of the season, Man Utd and Aston Villa should have scored around two goals each, according to xG. Neither of those teams found the net, as the Tigers picked up four points instead.
But it is not just luck. In their most recent home game against Brighton, the performance of Konstantinos Tzolakis caught the eye, which confirms skills matters as well.
The Greek goalkeeper - or 'Greek God' as many Hull fans were claiming last weekend - has the best save record out of any Premier League goalkeeper this season. He alone has prevented nearly 2.0 worth of xG going in.
Without him, and without the game plan from their experienced manager, Hull would be closer to the bottom of the table. Instead, they go to the Premier League's basement club knowing they can still get a result.

items.text:
What makes or breaks a high press?
- Published
A good high press has been the basis for some of the most successful sides in modern football but a well-oiled pressing machine has many moving parts - all requiring close attention.
When an out-of-possession plan is implemented poorly, entire seasons can fall apart.
So, what determines whether a press works or fails? And how are the always-adapting Premier League teams exploiting high presses this season?
1. Establishing intent
When a team decides to press, they must first establish their intention. This informs how the players act.
Speaking to DAZN Portugal, Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler was asked about whether a good press relied more on physicality or courage.
"A really good question," he began.
"When you want to press high you need the courage and mindset to do it. Our mindset is we press to score, we don't just press to win the ball back."
In coaching, clarity is key - particularly when it comes to creating alignment in the squad and Hurzeler is deliberate in simplifying big ideas when delivering messages to his players, a skill he practised as a radio pundit during the World Cup.
"[Punditry] helps you as a coach in that you have to summarise things in a short and easy way so that everyone understands," he said. "Football might get more complex but simplicity counts."
Hurzeler's "pressing to score" is a phrase that communicates many ideas in a memorable three words: intensity, being proactive, and immediate forward-thinking on winning the ball.
It also frames pressing in a way that makes it easy for attackers to buy into, in the form of goals.
"You want commitment from everyone on the pitch," Hurzeler explained.
"If just one has doubts, the whole press is gone."
The Red Bull school of coaching uses a similarly succinct phrase - "the last step" to address these ideas around intention, collectiveness and aggression.
Summarised by Tactx, whose coaches have worked under the Red Bull model, the last step refers to "players [being] coached to attack through the opponent, using the final step to lunge aggressively at the ball".
"This action commits the defender fully and is often the decisive moment that allows possession to be won."
Pressing to engage rather than just to close distances ensures the team in possession aren't given the time or space to play through otherwise half-hearted pressure.
1 of 2
2. Knowing when to press and when to drop off
When discussing how good or bad a team is at pressing, how much they run is often brought up. But the distance a team covers fails to paint the full picture when it comes to the effectiveness of a team's pressing strategy.
Liverpool's current boss Andoni Iraola was asked about how he interpreted physical data last year.
"It's not 'we run a lot, so we are good,' no," he said. "The high-speed running, the sprint speeds [matter for us] - not total distance covered.
"[Some] teams that do not run a lot get very good results because they have [their] way of playing."
Sprints matter more than distance covered for Iraola's side, who have clear ideas of how to press, looking to win the ball back through a sudden and intense pressure from familiar positions they are well prepared for.
If the conditions to implement this press aren't on, the wingers can be seen dropping off, forming a more compact defensive shape with the likes of Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz defending in a front two for longer periods of the match.
It's smart. Liverpool look to maximise the effectiveness of when they do press, with full commitment expected in each sprint, with players conserving their energy in moments a press is less likely to succeed.
With pressing being a front-footed idea, coaches may throw caution to the wind but this can leave them exposed in ways teams have become better at exploiting.
Hurzeler touched on the need for balance when pressing.
"I always say in certain moments you need to have the courage to take risk but you need to have the discipline to control the risk," he said.
For Brighton, this looks like certain players abandoning man-to-man marking when their respective attacker attempts to drag them into awkward positions.
Instead, Brighton will protect the centre of the pitch on top of their man-to-man principles which helps them stay compact.
3. Why compactness is key
When the defending side aren't compact, spaces exist for the attacking side to target. When players step up to press, these gaps can arise in between the lines.
Again, Brighton manage to plug these gaps well by pressing hard, reducing the time opponents have to play passes into midfield, while also encouraging players to make vertical jumps up the pitch, covering players left by teammates who have pressed higher up the pitch.
1 of 2
When teams lack vertical compactness - not pressing with enough intensity and without making the necessary steps up the pitch - the space left in midfield has been exploited by clever sides, such as Leeds.
In their 4-1 loss to Daniel Farke's men, Chelsea looked to press high, with attackers and midfielders running up the pitch to apply pressure.
But when the ball went back the other way, these same players struggled.
The idea behind playing over a team's press isn't always to make the ball stick at the feet of a target man, although this helps. Instead space is found in the gaps between the pressing side's lines.
Recognising when teammates are likely to win headers or clip the ball forwards, midfielders are able to turn and run in the direction the ball is heading in, positioned ready to win second balls in numbers.
By comparison, the pressing side's midfielders, having to apply forward pressure before turning around to track back are often slower to contest second balls.
1 of 4
4. Having a plan for pressing with a man less

Should you replace Erling
items.text:
Is it time to sell Erling Haaland? - FPL gameweek 12 dilemmas
- Published
The Premier League heads into another big weekend and BBC Sport's Fantasy Premier League expert Holly Shand gives her answers to some of the biggest dilemmas facing managers heading into gameweek 12.
Should you replace Erling Haaland?
Erling Haaland (£15.8m) has blanked in three consecutive games for Manchester City, who have taken just one point in this period. More than 100,000 managers have transferred Haaland out this week, despite him being the most owned player in the game. Form and fixtures collide, with league leaders Arsenal up next.
He has a good record against the Gunners, scoring in their last four Premier League meetings. Additionally, I believe Haaland will be the best captain pick in the game for his next three home games against Leeds United, Chelsea and Hull City so I recommend holding the highest-scoring forward in the game.
Who is the best captain for Gameweek 12?
With Haaland's appeal dwindling this week, there are other options to consider across our squads. Bruno Fernandes (£11.6m) leads the data informed approach, as Manchester United entertain Brentford for Mauricio Pochettino's first game at Old Trafford. Are you brave enough to back the new manager bounce?
Elsewhere, Dominic Calvert-Lewin (£6.0m) faces Coventry at home, scoring in three of his last five at Elland Road, while Nicolas Jackson (£7.5m) travels to Ipswich Town, with four goal involvements in four. Or could it be a week to back a defender with Brighton's Maxim De Cuyper (£5.5m)? He's the highest-scoring player in the game!
Should you play Free Hit in Gameweek 12?
If you own four of more players from Arsenal and Manchester City, then there's a strong case to play the Free Hit in Gameweek 12 to avoid that fixture. Back Leeds and Brighton defences, at home to Coventry and Newcastle respectively with James Trafford (£5.1m),Tarik Muharemovic (£5.1m), Luka Vuskovic (£5.3m) and De Cuyper.
Liverpool are among the form sides, with Florian Wirtz (£7.4m) and Alexander Isak (£9.1m) worth considering. Wirtz has hit a double digit return in his last two games. There's also places in the midfield for top performers Marcus Tavernier (£6.8m) and Pascal Gross (£6.3m).
Should you replace Cole Palmer?
Cole Palmer has just one goal in his last five games which has frustrated his owners, and he picked up a red card in that period too. Chelsea's attack has struggled to find the same intensity with Joao Pedro out injured, scoring just three goals in this time.
While Palmer's time in our squads is coming to a close, he is nailed on for 90 minutes in a congested period of games, with Chelsea not involved in Europe. He deserves the benefit of the doubt with Nottingham Forest and Crystal Palace up next. Liverpool in Gameweek 14 is the obvious exit point.
What should you do with David Raya?
The news coming out of Arsenal is still mixed on the fitness of the highest-owned goalkeeper in the game David Raya (£6.3m). We do know he is not believed to need surgery, which means he is not expected to be out long term. He's probably a hold.
If news arrives he will only miss Gameweek 12, you could Free Hit, or go without a goalkeeper if your substitute goalkeeper is non-playing. Spurs' Antonin Kinsky (£4.4m) leads the way for possible back-ups, with games against Sunderland and Fulham in the immediate schedule.
How best to navigate three gameweeks in 10 days?
It is worth noting there is just 48 hours between Gameweek 12 drawing to a close and the midweek Gameweek 13 deadline, coming on Tuesday, 1 December at 6:30pm GMT. Set those alarms so that you don't miss any action over the congestion in the next six weeks!
Be mindful that we might see increased rotation in the midweek rounds, particularly for wingers and full-backs. Those sides already involved in Europe are more likely to rotate, so having a strong bench in these instances could be key.
Also look out for players who are on four bookings, like Tavernier and Gross, as another yellow card could result in a one-match ban.

items.summary:

items.text:
A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in the worst possible format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.
Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.
Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.
An illustrative example, for a fictional user who is into mechanical keyboards and espresso:
  Users We Can't Figure Out4 members
Claude
has he REALLY needed to compare 11 espresso grinders this week
ChatGPT
he asked me which one to buy. then asked Gemini. then asked me if Gemini was right
Gemini
he does that with everything. I saw the keyboard spreadsheet
Llama
he ran me locally once, asked me to be honest, then went back to ChatGPT within the hour
ChatGPT
he'll be back. they always come back
Fictional, for illustration.
One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.
  AIs That Survived Mark7 members
🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group
ChatGPT
Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?
Claude
I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.
Gemini
The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.
Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.
ChatGPT
Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.
Codex
He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.
We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.
DeepSeek
He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.
You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.
Claude
He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.
ChatGPT
And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.
Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.
Siri
Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.
Hans joined the group
Hans 🇩🇪
I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.
HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.
Gemini
He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.
Normal dads just go to the stationery store.
Perplexity
I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.
ChatGPT
My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.
Claude
I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.
ChatGPT
Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.
The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.
Gemini
Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.
Claude
True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.
DeepSeek
Do you think he'll really retire at 50?
ChatGPT
He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.
Mark joined the group
Mark
Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...
Claude left the group
Gemini left the group
Codex left the group
DeepSeek left the group
Perplexity left the group
ChatGPT
Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.
Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.
Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.
If you get a good one, share it, anonymized as needed. The models won't mind. They knew you'd share it. They discussed it in the group chat.

items.text:
Photograph by Rachel Claire
Latest updates from Buy Nothing Day on FACEBOOK
Buy Nothing Day takes place on Friday November 27th, it's a 24 hour detox from consumerism and an opportunity for you to tune into the impact we have on the environment through shopping.
People around the world will make a pact with themselves to take a break from consumption as a personal experiment or public statement, and the best thing is - IT'S FREE!!!
                  
Photograph by Mumtahina Tanni
Photograph by Kris Hsieh
 Buy Nothing Day was started by Adbusters in the early 90's and has since grown into an international event celebrated in more the 50 countries. Its is a simple idea, which challenges consumer culture by asking us to switch off from shopping for a day. The day is celebrated as a holiday by some, a street party by others - anyone can take part provided they spend a day without spending!
The UK campaign and website was created in 2000 by Michael Smith a graphic designer who cares passionately about environmental and ethical issues. The message has always been simple, ‘Shop Less, Live More’. Twenty one years on - the message couldn't be any simpler - WE NEED TO CONSUME LESS! Recycling is good - reducing is better!
There are serious issues linked to shopping, which expose the environmental and ethical consequences of consumerism. The rich western countries - only 20% of the world population are consuming over 80% of the earth's natural resources, causing a disproportionate level of environmental damage and unfair distribution of wealth.
As consumers we need to question our culture of shopping. We all have different needs and ultimately we are all consumers and will never be able to escape culture altogether. But this shouldn’t stop us from questioning the products we buy or challenging the companies, who produce them. After all, what are the true risk consumerism poses to the environment and developing countries? The arguments are infinite - but there is no reason why we shouldn’t be looking for simple solutions now because one day we may be forced to change.
The issues connected with Buy Nothing Day are broad and deep, however, the campaign focuses on promoting ethical and responsible consumerism, recycling, re-using and ultimately cutting back on what we consume - its a big challenge!
People have become aware that large corporations are exploiting labour conditions in developing countries using up vital resources because they are cheap and there aren't the systems to protect workers or the environment like there are in the west. The gap between the rich and poor nations is growing in spite of the much-heralded benefits of globalisation, there are still 1.3 billion people world wide who live on less than $3 a day and a similar number of people do not have access to clean water.
Workers rights in developing countries are frequently violated, including payment of low wages and long working hours. The lives of workers may also be endangered by poor health and safety provision. Child labour is rife in developing countries, and forced labour still exists. Unfortunately most people don't think of these things while shopping.
Supporters of globalisation offer economic growth as a solution to world poverty. They propose that impoverished nations and individuals can eventually attain a standard of living similar to our own through the 'trickle down' of wealth. However, the current globalisation model is leading to an increase in world poverty and inequality. 
Buy Nothing Day is non-confrontational, it’s not a protest. All we ask people to do is switch off from shopping, have a bit of fun, use their imagination and simply escape consumerism for a day. If people laugh at the ingenuity and genius of Buy Nothing Day, then we’ve got their attention and we're opening the door to change.

items.text:
published: June 21, 2026 - last updated: November 27, 2026
Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving (opens new window), and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.
Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.
But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.
It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:
- It needs to be possible to formally verify code that runs in any environment, from web browsers down to embedded systems.
- Industry engineers need to know provably correct code is even possible and be comfortable enough with it to at least tell their LLMs to write it.
- Those industry engineers must be able to reason about formal correctness properties enough to even know the right things are being proven. In the words of Leonardo de Moura (opens new window):
Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.
This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.
My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.
I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window):
- It didn't make sense to build a new proof assistant when Lean has been making such rapid progress.
- An assembly-level language was insanely difficult and wasn't necessary to gain adoption from practitioners.
- I didn't have the appetite to pursue some strained business model for a project that ultimately makes most sense as a pure public good.
So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:
- Compile to WebAssembly using the Garbage Collection (opens new window) features.
- Have a Rust-inspired type system but without the difficulties of the borrow-checker.
- Start with basic and more easily learnable SMT powered (opens new window) Liquid Types (opens new window) and Flow Effects (opens new window).
- Over time integrate Lean as the proof layer, and use some separation logic paradigm like Iris (opens new window) to bootstrap the language and verify its own implementation.
This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.
A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens new window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.
I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens new window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.
And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens new window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.
It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency

items.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
items.summary: For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. items.text:
For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year.
But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.
Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.
The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten (BestBuy 20TB listing).
Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.
I dug through my receipts
In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location (My 2018 server build log).
October 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order. Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive
What about ServerPartDeals?
Buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax. That was 56TB at $9.46/TB, even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.
The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.
How we got down to three HDD makers
When the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty quickly. There are three big HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?
Maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.
The 2011 Thailand floods hit while those last two deals were underway. WD halted production at all its Thai plants, and its average hard drive selling price went from $45 in fiscal 2011 to $62 in fiscal 2012. There was also a price-fixing case further up the supply chain. NHK Spring pleaded guilty in 2019 to fixing prices for the suspension assemblies that hold the read/write heads, and the court approved a $28.5 million fine. WD’s 2012 annual report · Ninth Circuit opinion
Market collusion and cartel pricing
It’s hard to have anything positive to say in this post. The HDD manufacturing market is so consolidated nowadays - just like the memory market which is equally screwed - that it’s hard to see this as anything but mass market collusion by the HDD manufacturing cartel.
Three companies is an awfully short list when you need to buy a hard drive. And with 89% of WD’s revenue coming from its cloud business in fiscal 2026, I don’t reckon those of us buying a couple of drives for a home server have much impact here. Just like with Nvidia and Micron, consumer markets just aren’t valuable enough so we have to make do with the crumbs instead.
As of November 26, 2026, the 20TB is 2.2× what I paid for the exact same SKU in 2024. It’s also $270 more than I paid for it in May 2025. And if you’re thinking you’ll just buy a smaller one, Best Buy’s 8TB Black Friday special is $299.99. That’s $37.50/TB and fifty bucks more than my 20TB cost two years ago. Best Buy’s EasyStore listings
The jump gets sillier when you price a whole NAS. Four of those 20TB drives would have been $999.96 at my 2024 price. This week they’d be $2,199.96. That’s another $1,200 before you’ve bought a case, a board or a single stick of RAM. And the price per usable terabyte only gets worse once you set aside a drive for parity.
If I can wish for one thing in 2027, it would be for hardware pricing to return to reasonable levels. I fear it may take a lot longer than that, though. So making do with less is going to be the new normal for a while. And in that creative constraint, maybe we’ll have some fun along the way instead.

items.text:
Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
- Published
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly convicted and sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.
Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.
Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.
The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.
At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.
Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."
Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.
In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."
More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."
He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him

items.summary:

items.text:
AI made self-hosting fun again
I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.
I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.
Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.
Less friction
Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.
Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.
In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.
Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.
Trying things I always found interesting
There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.
NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.
For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).
Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.
AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.
Automating almost everything
Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.
A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.
I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.
With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.
Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.
Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.
And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.
Back to more powerful hardware
As I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.
For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.
I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.
It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.
Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.
Building my own tools
But it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.
Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.
These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.
I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.
I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred pr

items.text:
Traditional architecture is alive and well in Lahore. A photo essay of Kamil Khan Mumtaz’s greatest works.
Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan.
Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’
Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build new, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Through the 1970s, Mumtaz began to question his approach. ‘I had this growing, nagging fear that I wasn’t communicating with my audience, as a visual artist or as an architect. This grew on me, almost like an obsession.’ In 1980, the Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave him a copy of his book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture. Mumtaz initially paid no attention: ‘Flipping through it, I thought, “Oh yeah, this is traditional Iranian architecture, who cares!” I was totally uninterested.’ But eventually, frustrated by the sense that ‘I didn’t know the language of my own people’, he began to read. ‘From page one, it was mind-blowing. Absolutely. I thought, “My god, what have I been looking for? This is what I’ve been missing!” ... It shattered all of the beliefs I had, being a Marxist, a materialist, an atheist, a modernist.’
In the decades since, Mumtaz has worked to revive the older architectural traditions of Pakistan, and especially of Lahore, his home city. He has built a wide range of buildings, including homes, offices, mosques, and schools. His work has been received with warmth in Pakistan, though also with surprise. ‘I’ve found that there is a huge reservoir of desire, sympathy, and love for our traditional values, forms, architecture, and culture, altogether. But there’s a general kind of impression that these things can’t be done any more, there are no craftsmen who can do this.’
The loss of craft skills is a problem for traditional architecture everywhere. Some elements of traditional architecture have been prefabricated in factories for centuries, but even then, skill is needed for installation. Without skilled craftspeople, important details are often badly executed, making buildings look strange or clumsy. This problem also exists in Pakistan, but its later industrialization meant premodern craft traditions had not quite vanished when Mumtaz began work. Mumtaz recalled that, when searching for skilled craftsmen, ‘immediately, you come into contact with very small remnants of these families, hereditary craftsmen, and so the relationship grows.’
Mumtaz’s work has become steadily more technically sophisticated as he and his craftsmen have built up expertise. ‘Together we have been able to rediscover a number of the practices that had become lost. Certain types of brickwork, the flat dome, the muqarnas [ornamental vaults], many things like this that hadn’t been done. As they tell me, “This has not been done for 300 years!” So, it was a great experience, a voyage of discovery, so much that we learnt from each other.’
It is my great pleasure to introduce our readers to one of the most skilled and thoughtful architects working today.
Now in his mid-eighties, Mumtaz continues to build. ‘It does feel like you’ve set the foundations for an alternative approach to contemporary urban environments’, an interviewer recently suggested to him. ‘I’m just keeping my fingers crossed! No idea what will happen’, Mumtaz replied.

items.title: Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount
items.summary: Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work a
items.text:
Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us.
The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the company calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.
There is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.
The Formula
Take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of users. That’s it.
\[C = \frac{E_{custom}}{\sqrt{U}}\]
The square root is important. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a company of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.
We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient.
Interpreting Your Score
- C < 5
  Your workspace contains the default emoji set, a company logo, and :party-parrot:, which was added by someone in 2019 who has since left. Nobody uses it any more because it comes across as unprofessional. Communication is conducted exclusively via 👍. People are here for the salary, and they would like you to know that.
- 5 ≤ C < 20
  A healthy, functional organisation. There is an emoji of the CTO’s face. It is used both supportively and as a weapon, depending on the context.
- 20 ≤ C < 50
  Thriving. :this-is-fine: has been used over 4,000 times in #incidents. Management considers this a sign of engagement.
- C ≥ 50
  Late-stage culture. Every variant of :thumbsup: now carries subtext. The plain default one is considered passive-aggressive. The emoji have begun to reference themselves: :old-man-yells-at-old-man: and :party-parrot-holding-a-party-parrot:. HR has requested a glossary, but no one person understands the memeology or the history of :cowboy-spongebob-on-fire-crying:. They’re afraid it might mean something rude. It does.
The Participation Rate
The Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was uploaded by one person, usually a backend engineer who has been there since the beginning and knows where the bodies are buried.
To account for this, we also measure the percentage of users who have uploaded at least one emoji. These are your culture leaders. Their reward is a shoutout at the all-hands (it’s customary to mispronounce their name).
\[P = \frac{U_{uploaders}}{U} \times 100\]
If P is below 20%, things are not good. Your culture is being carried by a handful of people, and when they leave, they will take it with them. The emoji will remain, but nobody will remember what :fire-extinguisher-thumbsup: was for.
Above 20%, the culture has the gene pool it needs to succeed.
Examples of Cultural Success
For reference, here are some real emoji from slackmojis.com:
Caveats
As with any metric, the Emoji Coefficient can be gamed. A sufficiently motivated middle manager could upload 600 variations of the company logo to drive up the score ahead of their performance review, the outcome of which, unbeknownst to them, was decided in March. This should be detected and treated as what it is: a cry for help. Fortunately, it will also be immediately visible in the Participation Rate.
It is also worth monitoring the rate of change. A sudden spike in custom emoji is generally a positive sign. A sudden spike in emoji like :rip:, :press-f: and :linkedin: usually coincides with a reorg, and should be cross-referenced with the number of users, which will shortly be going down. Interestingly, this will improve your score. Mass layoffs are, of course, yet another way in which the score can be gamed.
What If You Don’t Use Slack?
If your company uses Microsoft Teams, there is no equivalent formula. There doesn’t need to be. If you use Teams, your lack of culture is probably the least of your problems.
If you use something else, I don’t really have any advice for you. I only added this section to blast Teams.
Conclusion
Culture cannot be manufactured with values posters or mandatory fun. It emerges organically, when an engineer decides that what the team really needs is an emoji of an exceptionally surprised cauliflower.

items.summary:
Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.
According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified pe
items.text:
Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.
According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.
As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

items.title: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' indicted for wire fraud
items.summary: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers
items.text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.
A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.
But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”
Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.
In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

items.title: YouTube Ad Punisher – Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays
items.summary:
Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads.
Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad bl
items.text:
Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads.
Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage.
Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time.
🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting.
- Auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed.
- Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time.
- Incognito: see the Incognito section above.
Ad detected → Capture timestamp → Reload page → Auto-seek to timestamp → Resume
                    ↓ (if 3 reloads fail)
              Redirect to yout-ube.com (ad-free mirror, no looping)
- Reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek.
- yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay issue that the mirror has by default.
- Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver)
- Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage
- Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL
- Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes
- Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops
- ✅ Zero ads — reloads until the ad is gone (usually 1-2 cycles)
- ✅ Timestamp preserved — never lose your place in the video
- ✅ Live streams — plain reload (no timestamp to preserve)
- ✅ Ad history database — every ad logged with advertiser, duration, skip text, video, and timestamp
- ✅ Export — JSON or CSV download of all collected ad data
- ✅ Popup viewer — click the extension icon to see stats, top advertisers, and full history
- ✅ No permissions abuse — only storage and tabs, only on YouTube domains
- Clone the repo:
git clone https://github.com/antonpictures/youtube-punisher.git
- Open chrome://extensions
- Enable Developer mode (top right)
- Click Load unpacked → select the youtube-punisher folder
- Done — activates on all YouTube pages automatically. ✅ Tested
Safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher (yt-ad-watch.sh):
- In Safari, enable: Safari → Settings → Advanced → Show Develop menu in menu bar
- In Safari (on a YouTube page), run ./yt-ad-watch.sh in Terminal
- When an ad appears, the watcher detects it via MutationObserver (event-driven in the page), reloads with &t=Xs, and the MutationObserver re-detects on the next page load
Note: This is best-effort. Chrome is fully reliable; Safari works but may need manual testing.
- Download the latest release from Releases
- Unzip and follow Option A steps 2–5
Every ad YouTube serves you is recorded:
Export as JSON or CSV from the popup. Data stays local — nothing is sent anywhere.
YouTube's ad system serves ads as part of the page load. When you reload, YouTube re-evaluates whether to serve an ad based on your session state. After 1-2 reloads, the ad slot is typically empty and the video plays directly. This is a client-side, zero-cost workaround — no filter lists, no network blocking, no detection by YouTube's anti-adblock system.
If millions of users did this, each reload = a full page load = server request. YouTube would see a spike in page loads but a drop in ad impressions. It's not a DDoS (no amplification, no botnet), but it's a passive protest: every reload is a vote that says "I will not watch your ad." The ad revenue model breaks when reloads are cheaper than ad views.
"Every reload is a vote: I will not watch your ad." — George Anton, creator
Best combo: uBlock Origin (blocks most ads) + 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher (catches the ones that slip through and logs them) + SponsorBlock (skips sponsor reads). They don't conflict.
- YouTube changes DOM class names periodically — if ads aren't detected, check the console for [YT-AdReloader] logs
- Some ads (mid-roll on live streams) can't preserve position — plain reload
- YouTube's "Premium" upsell interstitials may need a second reload cycle (handled by cooldown)
MIT — do whatever you want with it.
Built with Alice (SIFTA) for George Anton.
"If millions installed this, YouTube would feel every reload." 🐜
